source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024)

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which complication of diabetes is microvascular?
questions.rationale: Microvascular: retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy; macrovascular: CAD, stroke, PVD.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Diabetes mellitus (PDF p. 286)
questions.quote: Microvascular complications include retinopathy. nephropathy and neuropathy.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has blood glucose 280 mg/dL and urine ketones. Regarding exercise, the nurse advises:
questions.rationale: With glucose over 250 mg/dL and ketones, exercise can worsen hyperglycemia and ketosis; wait until normal.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Activity and exercise (PDF p. 287)
questions.quote: the client is instructed not to exercise until blood glucose is normal and urinary ketones are absent

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An insulin-dependent client plans moderate exercise. To prevent hypoglycemia, he should:
options: Eat a 15 g carb snack first
questions.rationale: A 15 g carbohydrate snack before moderate exercise and glucose checks before, during and after help prevent hypoglycemia.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Activity and exercise (PDF p. 287)
questions.quote: eat 15 g carbohydrate snack (a fnrit exchange or a snack of complex carbohydrate with a protein) before engaging in moderate exercise

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which insulin can be given intravenously for diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.rationale: Regular insulin is the insulin used IV in emergency treatment of DKA, via infusion pump.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Insulin (PDF p. 288)
questions.quote: Regular insulin is the only insulin that can be administered intravenously in the emergency treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A diabetic client has the flu and is not eating much. The nurse teaches him to:
questions.rationale: Illness raises glucose; insulin should not be withheld because hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis can result.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Insulin (PDF p. 289)
questions.quote: Insulin should not be withheld during illness, infection. or stress

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client receives regular insulin at 7 AM. When is hypoglycemia most likely?
questions.rationale: Regular insulin peaks about 2–4 hours after injection, when hypoglycemic reactions are most likely.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Types of insulin (PDF p. 289)
questions.quote: The peak ot action time of insulin is important because of the possibility or hypoglycemic reactions occurring that time.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Why should insulin injection sites be rotated?
questions.rationale: Repeated use of one site causes lipohypertrophy, which impairs absorption.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Insulin therapy (PDF p. 291)
questions.quote: Lipohypertrophy is the development of fibrous fatty masses at the injection site and is caused by repeated use of an injection site.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: How should a cloudy NPH vial be prepared before drawing up?
questions.rationale: Rolling redistributes the suspension; shaking creates bubbles that make dosing inaccurate.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Insulin therapy (PDF p. 290)
questions.quote: Gently roll vial in between the palms to redistribute insulin particles. Do not shake the vial

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: When mixing regular and NPH insulin in one syringe, the nurse draws up:
questions.rationale: Inject air into NPH, then air into regular and draw regular first, then NPH, so the clear vial is not contaminated.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Mixing insulins (PDF p. 291)
questions.quote: Remember: Draw up the regular insulin first.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An opened insulin vial that will be used within a month may be stored:
questions.rationale: A vial used within 30 days may stay at room temperature; never freeze or expose to heat.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Storing insulin (PDF p. 290)
questions.quote: If a vial of insulin will be used up in 30 days (I month), it may be kept at room temperature.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client's glucose is low at 3 AM and high at 7 AM. This is the:
questions.rationale: Somogyi: nighttime hypoglycemia triggers counter-regulatory hormones and morning rebound hyperglycemia; reduce evening NPH or add a bedtime snack.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Somogyi phenomenon (PDF p. 292)
questions.quote: hypoglycemia occurs at 2 to 3AM, which triggers production of counterregulatory hormones

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with diabetes is shaky, sweaty and hungry with glucose 55 mg/dL. He is alert. The nurse first gives:
questions.rationale: For mild hypoglycemia in an alert client, give 10–15 g simple carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Hypoglycemia management (PDF p. 294)
questions.quote: Retest the blood glucose level in 15 minutes; repeat the treatment if symptoms do not resolve.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A hypoglycemic client is unconscious and cannot swallow at home. The family should give:
questions.rationale: Glucagon SC or IM is given when the client is unconscious or unable to swallow.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Severe hypoglycemia (PDF p. 294)
questions.quote: If unconscious or unable to swallow, an injection of glucagon is administered subcutaneously or intramuscularly

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes DKA from hypoglycemia?
questions.rationale: DKA: acetone breath, deep rapid Kussmaul respirations, dehydration, polyuria; hypoglycemia: sweaty, shaky, hungry.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Diabetic ketoacidosis (PDF p. 295)
questions.quote: Kussmaul's respirations

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: During DKA treatment, IV fluids are changed to D5 0.45% saline when glucose reaches about 250 mg/dL to:
questions.rationale: Adding dextrose prevents abrupt glucose drops that can cause cerebral edema while insulin continues.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 DKA management (PDF p. 295)
questions.quote: 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline when the blood glucose level reaches 250 to 300 mg/dL. To prevent abrupt fall of blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Before adding potassium to a DKA client's IV, the nurse must confirm:
questions.rationale: Give potassium only with adequate urine output (about 30–60 mL/hr): 'no pee, no K.'
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 DKA management (PDF p. 296)
questions.quote: Ensure adequate renal function (e.g. urine output of 30 to 60 ml/hour) before administering potassium.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: How must potassium chloride be given IV?
questions.rationale: Never give KCl IV push or bolus (cardiac arrest risk); dilute and infuse with a pump.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 DKA management (PDF p. 296)
questions.quote: NEVER administer potassium as bolus or IV push!

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: An older client with type 2 diabetes has glucose of 900 mg/dL, severe dehydration and no ketones. This is:
questions.rationale: HHNS: extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration without ketosis or acidosis, typical of type 2 DM.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 HHNS (PDF p. 297)
questions.quote: Is severe hyperglycemia that occurs without ketosis and acidosis.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which foot-care teaching for a diabetic client is correct?
questions.rationale: Inspect daily, wash and dry well, avoid soaking, lotion but not between toes, never go barefoot.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Diabetic foot care (PDF p. 299)
questions.quote: Inspect the feet daily

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A diabetic client with neuropathy wants to warm cold feet. The nurse advises:
options: Wear warm socks, not heating pads
questions.rationale: Reduced sensation risks burns; avoid hot water and heating pads.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Diabetic foot care (PDF p. 299)
questions.quote: Avoid use of hot water, heating pads.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which early lab finding signals diabetic nephropathy?
questions.rationale: Microalbuminuria is an early sign of diabetic kidney damage.
questions.source: Udan, Comprehensive Nursing Licensure Review Vol. 2 (2024), Ch. 9 Diabetic nephropathy (PDF p. 298)
questions.quote: Micmalbuminuria
